metadata.title: Some measures of finite groups related to permutation bases

extraction_notes.note: Sentence both asserts that f' is monotonic and introduces the term 'monotonic'; typed claim, though it also serves as the definition of monotonic used in ClP2 and ClP3.
Remark or algorithm: the greedy choice of an irredundant base is a one-line procedure stated as an aside; kept as a remark with no steps.

Single sentences (or one itemized list) introduce two or three terms at once (mu and independent; irredundant and minimal; meet- and join-semilattice; b_1,b_2,b_3); one node each, since the split rule cannot cut inside a sentence.

'Now it is clear that ...' is an immediate sentence; appending it to the preceding claim step would put the direction's conclusion inside the claim, so it was joined to the following step (the one-sentence reverse implication) instead.

Cited facts with no stated content (Diaconis and Saloff-Coste on product replacement, Cameron and Cara finding all independent generating sets of size n-1, Jerrum's algorithmic remark) were left as text, not nodes.
Source typos kept verbatim: 'K_J\cap K_J' for K_I\cap K_J, 'all the subgroups K_i are distinct' meaning K_I, 'is is', 'wwhere', 'fo'; proof environments are a custom pf theorem-style environment.

nodes.name: Monotonic closure f'
nodes.statement: If $f$ is a function from (isomorphism classes of) finite groups to natural numbers, let $f'$ be the function defined by \[f'(G)=\max\{f(H):H\le G\}.\]
nodes.statement_short: For a group invariant $f$, $f'(G)$ is the maximum of $f$ over all subgroups of $G$.

nodes.name: f' is monotonic
nodes.statement: The function $f'$ is necessarily monotonic: that is, if $H\le G$, then $f'(H)\le f'(G)$.

nodes.name: Monotonic functions satisfy f = f'
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $f$ is monotonic, then $f=f'$; so every monotonic function is of this form.
conclusions: every monotonic function is of this form

nodes.name: Minimum number of generators d(G)
nodes.statement: An obvious function is $d(G)$, the minimum number of generators of $G$.

nodes.name: Symmetric groups are 2-generated
nodes.statement: Now is is well-known that $d(S_n)=2$; so this invariant is not very sensitive.

nodes.name: Babai's question on d'(S_n)
nodes.statement: Babai~\cite{babai} raised the question of determining $d'(S_n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Determine the maximum over subgroups of $S_n$ of the minimum number of generators.

nodes.name: Subgroup chain length l(G)
nodes.statement: Babai considered the related function $l$, where $l(G)$ is the length of the longest chain of subgroups of $G$.
differentia: of the longest chain of subgroups of $G$

nodes.name: d'(G) <= l(G)
nodes.statement: Since, obviously, $d(G)\le l(G)$, and $l$ is monotonic, (that is, $l(G)=l'(G)$), we see that $d'(G)\le l(G)$ for any group $G$.

nodes.name: Babai's bound on subgroup chains in S_n
nodes.statement: Babai proved that \[d'(S_n)\le l(S_n)\le 2n-1.\]

nodes.name: Cameron-Solomon-Turull formula for l(S_n)
nodes.statement: The exact value of $S_n$ was established by Cameron, Solomon and Turull~\cite{cst}: \[l(S_n)=\left\lceil\frac{3n}{2}\right\rceil-b(n)-1,\] where $b(n)$ is the number of $1$s in the base~$2$ representation of $n$.
assumptions: $b(n)$ is the number of $1$s in the base~$2$ representation of $n$
nodes.statement_short: The longest subgroup chain in $S_n$ has length $\lceil 3n/2\rceil - b(n) - 1$, with $b(n)$ the binary digit sum of $n$.

nodes.name: Jerrum's bound d'(S_n) <= n-1
nodes.statement: Jerrum~\cite{jerrum} showed that $d'(S_n)\le n-1$.

nodes.name: McIver-Neumann theorem
nodes.statement: The exact value of $d'(S_n)$ was established by McIver and Neumann~\cite{mn}: \[d'(S_n)=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor\hbox{ for }n>3.\]

nodes.name: Independent set and mu(G)
nodes.statement: Whiston~\cite{whiston} considered the invariant $\mu(G)$, the maximal size of an independent generating set for $G$, where a set is \emph{independent} if none of its elements lies in the subgroup generated by the others.
nodes.genus: the maximal size of an independent generating set for $G$
differentia: none of its elements lies in the subgroup generated by the others
nodes.statement_short: $\mu(G)$ is the largest size of an independent generating set; a set is independent if no element lies in the subgroup generated by the rest.

nodes.name: mu'(G) is the maximum independent subset size
nodes.statement: Since any independent set is an independent generating set for the subgroup it generates, $\mu'(G)$ is the maximum size of an independent subset of $G$.
conclusions: $\mu'(G)$ is the maximum size of an independent subset of $G$

nodes.name: Whiston's theorem
nodes.statement: Whiston showed that \[\mu(S_n)=\mu'(S_n)=n-1.\]

nodes.name: Groups with mu'(G) > mu(G) exist
nodes.statement: However, he observed that there are groups with $\mu'(G)>\mu(G)$.

nodes.name: Base of a permutation group
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a permutation group on $\Omega$. A \emph{base} for $G$ is a sequence of points of $\Omega$ whose pointwise stabiliser is the identity.
differentia: whose pointwise stabiliser is the identity

nodes.name: Irredundant and minimal bases
nodes.statement: A base is called \emph{irredundant} if no point is fixed by the pointwise stabiliser of its predecessors; it is \emph{minimal} if no point is fixed by the pointwise stabiliser of the other points in the sequence.
differentia: no point is fixed by the pointwise stabiliser of its predecessors
no point is fixed by the pointwise stabiliser of the other points in the sequence

nodes.name: Greedy choice of an irredundant base
nodes.statement: It is computationally a simple matter to choose an irredundant base; simply choose each base point to be a point moved by the stabiliser of the points previously chosen. It is less straightforward to choose a minimal base.
nodes.statement_short: An irredundant base is found greedily by picking points moved by the current stabiliser; minimal bases are harder.

nodes.name: Minimal bases are those all of whose reorderings are irredundant
nodes.statement: Note that a base is minimal if and only if every re-ordering of it is irredundant.
conclusions: a base is minimal if and only if every re-ordering of it is irredundant

nodes.name: Base measures b_1, b_2, b_3
nodes.statement: Now, given a finite group $G$, we define three numbers $b_1(G)$, $b_2(G)$, $b_3(G)$ as follows. In each case, the maximum is taken over all permutation representations of $G$ (not necessarily faithful). \begin{itemize} \item $b_1(G)$ is the maximum, over all representations, of the maximum size of an irredundant base; \item $b_2(G)$ is the maximum, over all representations, of the maximum size of a minimal base; \item $b_3(G)$ is the maximum, over all representations, of the minimum base size. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Over all (not necessarily faithful) permutation representations: $b_1$ = max irredundant base size, $b_2$ = max minimal base size, $b_3$ = max of minimum base size.

nodes.name: PSL(2,7) separates the base measures
nodes.statement: These inequalities can be strict. The group $G=\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)$ has $b_1(G)=5$, $b_2(G)=4$, and $b_3(G)=3$.

nodes.name: b_1(G) equals the subgroup chain length
Proof of Proposition 2.2
nodes.statement: Given an irredundant base of size $b_1(G)$, the stabilisers of its initial subsequences form a properly descending chain of subgroups of length $b_1(G)$. So $b_1(G)\le l(G)$. Conversely, let \[G=G_0>G_1>\cdots>G_l=1\] be a chain of subgroups of length $l=l(G)$. Consider the action on the union of the coset spaces of the subgroups $G_i$, and let $\alpha_i$ be the point $G_i$ of the coset space $(G:G_i)$. Then $(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_l)$ is an irredundant base. So $l(G)\le b_1(G)$.\hfill$\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Two inequalities: an irredundant base gives a stabiliser chain; a subgroup chain gives an irredundant base in the action on the union of coset spaces.

nodes.name: Base gives a chain
nodes.statement: Given an irredundant base of size $b_1(G)$, the stabilisers of its initial subsequences form a properly descending chain of subgroups of length $b_1(G)$. So $b_1(G)\le l(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Stabilisers of initial segments of an irredundant base form a strict chain, so $b_1\le l$.

nodes.name: Chain gives a base
nodes.statement: Conversely, let \[G=G_0>G_1>\cdots>G_l=1\] be a chain of subgroups of length $l=l(G)$. Consider the action on the union of the coset spaces of the subgroups $G_i$, and let $\alpha_i$ be the point $G_i$ of the coset space $(G:G_i)$. Then $(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_l)$ is an irredundant base. So $l(G)\le b_1(G)$.\hfill$\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Act on the union of coset spaces of a maximal chain; the coset points form an irredundant base, so $l\le b_1$.

nodes.name: b_3 of simple groups is attained on primitive actions
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a non-abelian finite simple group. Then $b_3(G)$ can be calculated by considering only the primitive permutation representations of $G$.
assumptions: Let $G$ be a non-abelian finite simple group.
conclusions: $b_3(G)$ can be calculated by considering only the primitive permutation representations of $G$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.3
nodes.statement: Given any permutation representation of $G$, we can discard fixed points, so that $G$ acts faithfully on each orbit. Now let $b_3^*(G)$ be the maximum of the minimum base sizes over all transitive representations of $G$, and suppose that there is an intransitive representation with minimum base size greater than $b_3^*(G)$. Now there exist at most $b_3^*(G)$ points in an orbit whose stabiliser acts trivially on that orbit, and hence is trivial (since the action on the orbit is faithful), contrary to assumption. Now let $b_3^+(G)$ be the maximum of the minimum base sizes over all primitive representations of $G$, and suppose that there is a transitive but imprimitive representation with base size greater than $b_3^+(G)$. There are at most $b_3^+(G)$ maximal blocks whose stabiliser acts trivially on the block system, and hence is trivial (since again the action is faithful), contrary to assumption.\hfill$\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce from intransitive to transitive and from imprimitive to primitive actions, each time using faithfulness of the simple group's action on an orbit or block system.

nodes.name: Reduction to transitive actions
nodes.statement: Given any permutation representation of $G$, we can discard fixed points, so that $G$ acts faithfully on each orbit. Now let $b_3^*(G)$ be the maximum of the minimum base sizes over all transitive representations of $G$, and suppose that there is an intransitive representation with minimum base size greater than $b_3^*(G)$. Now there exist at most $b_3^*(G)$ points in an orbit whose stabiliser acts trivially on that orbit, and hence is trivial (since the action on the orbit is faithful), contrary to assumption.
nodes.statement_short: A base of one faithful orbit is a base for the whole action, so transitive representations suffice.

nodes.name: Reduction to primitive actions
nodes.statement: Now let $b_3^+(G)$ be the maximum of the minimum base sizes over all primitive representations of $G$, and suppose that there is a transitive but imprimitive representation with base size greater than $b_3^+(G)$. There are at most $b_3^+(G)$ maximal blocks whose stabiliser acts trivially on the block system, and hence is trivial (since again the action is faithful), contrary to assumption.\hfill$\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Maximal blocks giving a base of the faithful action on the block system give a base, so primitive representations suffice.

nodes.name: PSL(2,7) on points and lines: b_2 not attained on transitive actions
nodes.statement: This proposition does not hold for $b_2(G)$. For the group $G=\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)\cong\mathrm{PSL}(3,2)$, a minimal base in any transitive representation has size at most $3$. However, in the action on the points and lines of the projective plane of order~$2$, there is a minimal base of size~$4$, consisting of two points and two lines such that each point lies on one of the lines and each line passes through one of the points.
nodes.statement_short: For PSL(3,2), transitive actions have minimal bases of size at most 3, but the action on points and lines of the Fano plane has a minimal base of size 4.

nodes.name: Subgroup lattice L(G)
nodes.statement: The subgroups of the group $G$ form a lattice $L(G)$, with the operations $H\wedge K=H\cap K$ and $H\vee K=\langle H,K\rangle$.

nodes.name: Meet- and join-semilattices of L(G)
nodes.statement: A \emph{meet-semilattice} of $L(G)$ is a collection of subgroups containing $G$ and closed under $\wedge$, while a \emph{join-semilattice} is a collection of subgroups containing the trivial group $1$ and closed under $\vee$.
differentia: containing the trivial group $1$ and closed under $\vee$

nodes.name: Boolean lattice B(n)
nodes.statement: The \emph{Boolean lattice} $B(n)$ is the lattice of subsets of an $n$-set.

nodes.name: Boolean meet- and join-embeddings are equivalent
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group. Then $B(n)$ is embeddable as a meet-semilattice in $L(G)$ if and only if it is embeddable as a join-semilattice.
conclusions: $B(n)$ is embeddable as a meet-semilattice in $L(G)$ if and only if it is embeddable as a join-semilattice

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $B(n)$ is a join-semilattice of $L(G)$. Let $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then, for every subset $I$ of $N$, there is a subgroup $H_I$ of $G$, and $H_{I\cup J}=\langle H_i,H_j\rangle$ for any two subsets $I$ and $J$. Moreover, all these subgroups are distinct. In particular, $H_i\not\le H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$ for all $i$ (where $H_i$ is shorthand for $H_{\{i\}}$); else \[H_N=\langle H_i,H_{N\setminus\{i\}}\rangle=H_{N\setminus\{i\}},\] contrary to assumption. Let $K_i=H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$, and for any $I\subseteq N$, put \[K_I=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i,\] with the convention that $K_\emptyset=G$. We claim that all the subgroups $K_i$ are distinct. Suppose that two of them are equal, say $K_I=K_J$. By interchanging $I$ and $J$ if necessary, we may assume that there exists $i\in I\setminus J$. But then $H_i\le K_J$ while $H_i\not\le K_I$, a contradiction. Now it is clear that $K_J\cap K_J=K_{I\cap J}$, so we have an embedding of $B(n)$ as a meet-semilattice (where we have reversed the order-isomoprhism to simplify the notation). The reverse implication is proved by an almost identical argument.\hfill$\Box$
nodes.statement_short: From a join-embedding $H_I$, take intersections of the complements $K_i=H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$; distinctness follows by contradiction, giving a meet-embedding. The converse is symmetric.

nodes.name: Join-embedding and non-containment
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $B(n)$ is a join-semilattice of $L(G)$. Let $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then, for every subset $I$ of $N$, there is a subgroup $H_I$ of $G$, and $H_{I\cup J}=\langle H_i,H_j\rangle$ for any two subsets $I$ and $J$. Moreover, all these subgroups are distinct. In particular, $H_i\not\le H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$ for all $i$ (where $H_i$ is shorthand for $H_{\{i\}}$); else \[H_N=\langle H_i,H_{N\setminus\{i\}}\rangle=H_{N\setminus\{i\}},\] contrary to assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Index the join-embedding by subsets $H_I$ and show $H_i\not\le H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$.

nodes.name: Define K_I
nodes.statement: Let $K_i=H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$, and for any $I\subseteq N$, put \[K_I=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i,\] with the convention that $K_\emptyset=G$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $K_I$ as intersections of the $K_i=H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$.

nodes.name: Claim: the K_I are distinct
nodes.statement: We claim that all the subgroups $K_i$ are distinct. Suppose that two of them are equal, say $K_I=K_J$. By interchanging $I$ and $J$ if necessary, we may assume that there exists $i\in I\setminus J$. But then $H_i\le K_J$ while $H_i\not\le K_I$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Claim that the subgroups $K_I$ are pairwise distinct, proved by contradiction.

nodes.name: Suppose two coincide
nodes.statement: Suppose that two of them are equal, say $K_I=K_J$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $K_I=K_J$ for distinct $I,J$.

nodes.name: WLOG choose i in I minus J
nodes.statement: By interchanging $I$ and $J$ if necessary, we may assume that there exists $i\in I\setminus J$.
nodes.statement_short: Without loss of generality pick $i\in I\setminus J$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: But then $H_i\le K_J$ while $H_i\not\le K_I$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: $H_i$ lies in $K_J$ but not in $K_I$, contradiction.

nodes.name: Meet-embedding and reverse implication
nodes.statement: Now it is clear that $K_J\cap K_J=K_{I\cap J}$, so we have an embedding of $B(n)$ as a meet-semilattice (where we have reversed the order-isomoprhism to simplify the notation). The reverse implication is proved by an almost identical argument.\hfill$\Box$
nodes.statement_short: The $K_I$ are closed under intersection, giving a meet-embedding; the converse follows by the dual argument.

nodes.name: Semilattice embeddability differs from lattice embeddability
nodes.statement: Note that the conditions of the proposition are not equivalent to embeddability of $B(n)$ as a lattice. For example, if $G$ is the quaternion group of order $8$, then $B(2)$ is embeddable as both a meet-semilattice and a join-semilattice but not as a lattice.
nodes.statement_short: Embedding $B(n)$ as a meet/join-semilattice is weaker than as a lattice; the quaternion group $Q_8$ and $B(2)$ show this.

nodes.name: Boolean semilattice characterisations of mu' and b_2
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group. \begin{enumerate} \item The largest $n$ such that $B(n)$ is embeddable as a join-semilattice of $L(G)$ is $\mu'(G)$. \item The largest $n$ such that $B(n)$ is embeddable as a meet-semilattice of $L(G)$ in such a way that the minimal element is a normal subgroup of $G$ is $b_2(G)$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: The largest $n$ such that $B(n)$ is embeddable as a join-semilattice of $L(G)$ is $\mu'(G)$.
The largest $n$ such that $B(n)$ is embeddable as a meet-semilattice of $L(G)$ in such a way that the minimal element is a normal subgroup of $G$ is $b_2(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mu'(G)$ is the largest $n$ with $B(n)$ join-embedded in $L(G)$; $b_2(G)$ is the largest with $B(n)$ meet-embedded with normal bottom.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement: (a) Let $\{g_1,\ldots,g_n\}$ be an independent set in $G$, where $n=\mu'(G)$. Let $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then the subgroups $H_I=\langle g_i:i\in I\rangle$ form a join-semilattice of $G$ isomorphic to $B(n)$. Conversely, suppose that we have a join-semilattice given by the subgroups $H_I$ for $I\subseteq N$. Choose $g_i\notin H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$. Then clearly the elements $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ are independent. \smallskip (b) Let $(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$ be a minimal base for $G$ in some permutation representation. Let $K_i$ be the stabiliser of $\alpha_i$, and $K_I=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i$ for $I\subseteq N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then the subgroups $K_I$ form a meet-semilattice of $G$. The subgroup$ K_N$ is the kernel of the permutation representation (by definition of a base), and so is a normal subgroup of $G$. Conversely, suppose that we have a meet-semilattice given by the subgroups $K_I$ for $I\subseteq N$, such that $K_N$ is a normal subgroup fo $G$; the notation is chosen so that $K_I\cap K_J=K_{I\cup J}$. Now consider the permutation representation on the union of the coset spaces of the subgroups $K_i=K_{\{i\}}$. Since the intersection of all these subgroups is normal, it is the kernel of the representation, and the points corresponding to the subgroups $K_i$ form a base. It is minimal, since the intersection of fewer than $n$ of the subgroups is not equal to $K_N$.\hfill$\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Two-way constructions: independent sets give join-embeddings and back; minimal bases give meet-embeddings via point stabilisers, and back via coset actions.

nodes.name: (a) independent sets and join-semilattices
nodes.statement: (a) Let $\{g_1,\ldots,g_n\}$ be an independent set in $G$, where $n=\mu'(G)$. Let $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then the subgroups $H_I=\langle g_i:i\in I\rangle$ form a join-semilattice of $G$ isomorphic to $B(n)$. Conversely, suppose that we have a join-semilattice given by the subgroups $H_I$ for $I\subseteq N$. Choose $g_i\notin H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$. Then clearly the elements $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ are independent.
nodes.statement_short: Part (a): correspondence between independent sets and join-embedded Boolean lattices.

nodes.name: Independent set gives join-embedding
nodes.statement: (a) Let $\{g_1,\ldots,g_n\}$ be an independent set in $G$, where $n=\mu'(G)$. Let $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then the subgroups $H_I=\langle g_i:i\in I\rangle$ form a join-semilattice of $G$ isomorphic to $B(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Subgroups generated by subsets of an independent set form a join-semilattice isomorphic to $B(n)$.

nodes.name: Join-embedding gives independent set
nodes.statement: Conversely, suppose that we have a join-semilattice given by the subgroups $H_I$ for $I\subseteq N$. Choose $g_i\notin H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$. Then clearly the elements $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ are independent.
nodes.statement_short: Choosing $g_i\notin H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$ gives an independent set.

nodes.name: (b) minimal bases and meet-semilattices
nodes.statement: (b) Let $(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$ be a minimal base for $G$ in some permutation representation. Let $K_i$ be the stabiliser of $\alpha_i$, and $K_I=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i$ for $I\subseteq N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then the subgroups $K_I$ form a meet-semilattice of $G$. The subgroup$ K_N$ is the kernel of the permutation representation (by definition of a base), and so is a normal subgroup of $G$. Conversely, suppose that we have a meet-semilattice given by the subgroups $K_I$ for $I\subseteq N$, such that $K_N$ is a normal subgroup fo $G$; the notation is chosen so that $K_I\cap K_J=K_{I\cup J}$. Now consider the permutation representation on the union of the coset spaces of the subgroups $K_i=K_{\{i\}}$. Since the intersection of all these subgroups is normal, it is the kernel of the representation, and the points corresponding to the subgroups $K_i$ form a base. It is minimal, since the intersection of fewer than $n$ of the subgroups is not equal to $K_N$.\hfill$\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Part (b): correspondence between minimal bases and meet-embedded Boolean lattices with normal bottom.

nodes.name: Minimal base gives meet-embedding
nodes.statement: (b) Let $(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$ be a minimal base for $G$ in some permutation representation. Let $K_i$ be the stabiliser of $\alpha_i$, and $K_I=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i$ for $I\subseteq N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then the subgroups $K_I$ form a meet-semilattice of $G$. The subgroup$ K_N$ is the kernel of the permutation representation (by definition of a base), and so is a normal subgroup of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Intersections of point stabilisers of a minimal base form a meet-semilattice whose bottom is the kernel, hence normal.

nodes.name: Meet-embedding gives minimal base
nodes.statement: Conversely, suppose that we have a meet-semilattice given by the subgroups $K_I$ for $I\subseteq N$, such that $K_N$ is a normal subgroup fo $G$; the notation is chosen so that $K_I\cap K_J=K_{I\cup J}$. Now consider the permutation representation on the union of the coset spaces of the subgroups $K_i=K_{\{i\}}$. Since the intersection of all these subgroups is normal, it is the kernel of the representation, and the points corresponding to the subgroups $K_i$ form a base. It is minimal, since the intersection of fewer than $n$ of the subgroups is not equal to $K_N$.\hfill$\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Act on the union of coset spaces of the $K_i$; the coset points form a minimal base.

nodes.name: b_2(G) <= mu'(G)
nodes.statement: $b_2(G)\le\mu'(G)$ for any group $G$.

nodes.name: Is b_2(G) < mu'(G) ever strict?
nodes.statement: I do not know a group where the inequality is strict. Resolving this is equivalent to the following question. Let $n$ be maximal such that $B(n)$ is embeddable as a meet-semilattice of $L(G)$. Is there an embedding of $B(n)$ for which the minimal element is normal?
nodes.statement_short: Is there a group with $b_2(G)<\mu'(G)$; equivalently, can a maximal meet-embedded $B(n)$ always be chosen with normal bottom?

nodes.name: Base measures of the symmetric group
Proof of Corollary 3.4
nodes.statement: We have \[n-1\le b_3(S_n)\le b_2(S_n)\le \mu'(S_n)=n-1,\] wwhere the first inequality holds because any base in the natural representation has size $n-1$; the second is trivial; the third comes from the preceding Corollary; and the equality is Whiston's theorem.\hfill$\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich: the natural action gives $n-1\le b_3$, then $b_3\le b_2\le\mu'$ and Whiston's theorem $\mu'(S_n)=n-1$.
